parsed.same_study_reason: Both lists concern estimates of global temperature shocks on GDP, their persistence and long-run translation into climate damages and the social cost of carbon.

pairs.reason: Both question whether confidence intervals are valid for a short, parameter-rich time-series/local-projection setting. B3 states the inference-validity concern more generally and requests simulations; A1 specifies overlapping cumulative outcomes, persistence, and specification sensitivity.

Both raise finite-sample doubts about asymptotic confidence intervals in a heavily parameterized dynamic regression. A1 covers additional sources of inference fragility, whereas B5 focuses narrowly on observations relative to parameters.

Both concern the 10-year local-projection results. A1 questions inference and specification sensitivity at that horizon; B4 says the horizon is too short to establish longer-run effects and SCC implications.

Both address whether observed temperature shocks can support conclusions about sustained warming. A3 focuses on the mismatch between natural variability and anthropogenic warming, while B2 focuses on dynamic functional form and scaling beyond observed shock sizes.

Both question the long-run welfare/SCC translation beyond the directly estimated horizon. A4 gives a broader structural critique of the damage kernel and welfare model; B4 specifically asks for longer-run effects and SCC sensitivity.

Both concern how lag and persistence assumptions in the temperature-shock model affect estimated damages. B2 additionally raises nonlinear and permanent-effect specifications and out-of-sample calibration.
Both identify linear extrapolation from historical shocks of roughly 0.3°C to substantially larger warming as weakly supported. B2 also bundles lag and growth-effect specification concerns.

Both concern extrapolation in long-run damage and SCC claims. A9 emphasizes nonlinear temperature responses, tails, tipping points, and adaptation; B4 emphasizes that effects are observed only through ten years.
Both concern whether persistence and permanent-versus-level dynamic assumptions justify the long-run damage interpretation. B2 covers additional lag, nonlinearity, and calibration issues.

Both question the long-run mapping from a transient temperature shock to permanent-warming damages and the SCC. A10 is specific to estimated temperature persistence and the damage kernel, while B4 asks more broadly for longer-horizon evidence and sensitivity.

Both concern the reported confidence regions. A11 says they omit structural, external-validity, extrapolation, and measurement uncertainties; B3 questions their frequentist validity in a small, complex time-series setting.

Both concern whether the reported confidence intervals support the claimed precision. A11 targets unintegrated substantive uncertainty, whereas B5 targets finite-sample failure of asymptotic inference.
